title: A Schoolday Errand
premise: Ride past the places where Chicago's first classes met, on both sides of the river. Bring a made-up family's question about school. End with a notice in the newspaper dated today.

opening.text:
JAUNT: A SCHOOLDAY ERRAND. Your family has one question. Where could a child go to school? In this town, getting to school is half the lesson. A teacher named Granville Sproat remembered carrying the smaller children on his back. He did not trust them on the slippery board over the mud. Once he even fell into the mud with a child in his arms.

Ride past the places where Chicago's first classes met, on both sides of the river. End where the Democrat newspaper is printed. It has a notice dated today about building a real school house.

stops.text: On Michigan Street, a history book says John Watkins later taught school in a house here. Another book says the house was Richard Hamilton's home. Watkins started teaching in 1832 in a small log house. He had only twelve students at first. Chicago's schools started very small.

choices.label: Ask about a child of five
choices.consequence: The question is for the youngest child in the family.

choices.label: Ask about a child of ten
choices.consequence: The question is for a student ready for reading and math.

stops.narrative: Once a classroom, now a home again.

stops.text: Go down to the river bank east of Clark Street. A history book says a school house was built here in 1833. It was the first one built just for a school. Watkins did not remember it, though. By 1835 it was the North Side's public school. South of the river, Sproat's school met upstairs in the Baptist church. He said it was a very nice school, and the students listened and behaved well.

choices.label: Write down the north-bank school
choices.consequence: A school we know was open in 1835. But the river is between it and the stores.

choices.label: Keep looking for one nearer
choices.consequence: Your note stays blank for now.

stops.narrative: Compare what the history books agree on.

stops.text: Cross the river to State Street, near the old army land. A history book says Eliza Chappel taught a school for little children in a log house here in 1833 and 1834. Other books say different things. In 1834 her school moved into the Presbyterian church.
stops.narrative: This is where the town's youngest students first met.

stops.text: Go on to South Water and Clark Streets, where the Democrat was first printed. Today's paper has a notice. People will meet in the Presbyterian Church on 7 July at six o'clock to talk about building a school house. Money is tight. The town sold its school land in 1833. A history book says the sale was a big mistake. If the town had waited twenty years, it would have made a hundred times more.

choices.label: Copy out the District No. 4 notice
choices.consequence: The meeting's day, time and place go in your note.

choices.label: Leave the notice to the paper
choices.consequence: You copy nothing. The question goes home just as it came.

legs.note: South through Kinzie's Addition to the river bank just east of Clark; another chapter of Andreas puts the school a block west.
legs.story: The family's question rides with you, and so does the mud.

legs.note: Over the river to the west side of State Street.
legs.story: There is one more classroom to see, south of the river.

legs.note: West along the south side to the corner of South Water and Clark.

endings.text: You wrote down the north-bank school, and you copied the meeting notice for 7 July. That is two answers to one family question: a school already teaching, and one people still have to argue about.

You did not write down a school yet, but you copied the notice. The meeting is on 7 July, at six in the evening, at the Presbyterian Church. The meeting will decide if a school house is built. You plan to be there.
You wrote down the north-bank school. But the river is between it and the stores. That is a long way every morning for a child of five. Somebody may have to carry the little one, like Sproat did.
You wrote down the north-bank school. It is a walk and a river crossing each morning. That is not hard for a child of ten. Is there room for one more student? You will have to ask the teacher.
You wrote nothing down and copied nothing. The question goes home just as it came. The schools you passed are real, the meeting is next week, and the asking goes on.

keepsake.title: A Schooling Note
keepsake.text: A made-up note about one family's question about school in July 1835, and what you wrote down or copied. No real student, teacher's answer or cost is written on it.

evidence.text: Andreas has Eliza Chappel's infant school of 1833–34 in a log house just outside the military reservation, divided into school-room and lodging quarters.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, the schools chapter, the Eliza Chappel paragraph (archive.org scan p. 431, as read in docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 9).

evidence.text: An unfootnoted 2018 online history says Chappell opened her school in a small log house formerly used as a store, and that in 1834 it moved into the First Presbyterian Church at Lake and Clark.
evidence.locator: Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal, 19 January 2018, the paragraph beginning 'Chappell arrived in Chicago in June 1833' (accessed 2026-09-04).

evidence.text: The log house is placed on the west side of State Street between South Water and Lake; the lot is not documented, and other accounts put the school's first room at Lake and Market or at Lake and Clark.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives only 'just outside the military reservation', whose western line on the south side was State Street until February 1835. The structure record chooses a point inside that two-block strip and grades it reconstructed; the online history and the Beaubien-cabin reading disagree on the site, so the stop says other accounts differ and claims no front door.

evidence.text: On 1 July 1835 the log house is inferred to stand; the school had left it in 1834 and no source names anyone in it in 1835.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record's phase carries the house to 1835 as an inference about how long a sound log house lasts, and its occupants field ends Chappel's use in 1834. The stop therefore narrates the school as history and says nothing of who is inside.

evidence.text: Andreas has John Watkins employed by Colonels Hamilton and Owen in 1833 to teach near the old Indian agency-house, and later in a house on Michigan Street between Cass and Rush.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, archive.org scan p. 305 (as read in docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 9 and docs/research/03-structures-north.md).

evidence.text: Moses and Kirkland say Richard J. Hamilton, with Colonel Owen, hired John Watkins in 1833, and about then built his house on what is now Michigan Street between Cass and Rush, where he lived for nineteen years.
The house Watkins taught in and the house Hamilton built are read as one house on the north side of Michigan Street; its lot is not documented and no class in it in 1835 is recorded.
evidence.reasoning: The same employers, teacher, year and block face appear in both histories; neither names the other's house, and Moses and Kirkland give no side of the street. The structure record makes the identification as an inference, sets the house mid-face and grades the coordinate reconstructed, and its function says the school use is unattested by 1835.

evidence.text: Andreas reports from Mr. Wells's report that Hamilton and Owen built a house on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street, in which Watkins continued his school, the first house built for a school in Chicago, but adds that this does not recur to Watkins's recollection.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, the schools chapter, the paragraph citing Mr. Wells's report (as quoted in data/structures/north_side_school_1833.json and docs/RESEARCH/north_side_school_1833.md § 1).

evidence.text: Andreas says that in 1835 John Watkins was teaching what had become a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building Hamilton and Owen erected in 1833, and that the exact date of his retirement is not known.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, the schools chapter, the 1835 paragraph following George Davis's school in the Presbyterian church (archive.org scan p. 433, as read in docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 9).

evidence.text: The school-house is placed on the North Water Street frontage just east of Clark; Andreas's Methodist chapter puts 'the Watkins school-house' between Clark and LaSalle, about a block west.
evidence.reasoning: The schools chapter's 'just east of Clark Street' is adopted because it is the more specific statement, made twice, in the chapter about the building; the structure record keeps the other reading as a stated uncertainty, so the stop speaks of the bank and the year, not a door or a July class.

evidence.text: The Democrat's first issue, 26 November 1833, gives its office as the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets; John Calhoun printed it there.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), the imprint; Andreas vol. 1, the press chapter on Calhoun's office.

evidence.text: By 20 May 1835 the Democrat's colophon gives the office as over Messrs. Jones & King's hardware store, in South Water Street, so the corner is a former office on the scene date.
evidence.locator: 20 May 1835 (Vol. II No. 5), p. 4, col. 6, the colophon (transcription lines 4177–4180). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: The Democrat of 1 July 1835 prints a notice, dated 17 June: a meeting of the inhabitants of School District No. 4 will be held on Tuesday 7 July at 6 o'clock P.M. in the Presbyterian Church, to consider measures for building a school house in the district and to elect a trustee.
evidence.locator: 1 July 1835, p. 3, col. 5 (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_07_01#c012); first printed 17 June 1835, p. 3, col. 3 (chicago_democrat_1835_06_17#c006). Transcription-mediated reading of a damaged column.

evidence.text: Granville T. Sproat, the schoolmaster, remembered the village streets: 'It lay in many places half a leg deep, up to the hubs of the carts and wagons in the middle of the streets, and the only sidewalk we had was a single plank stretched from one building to another. The smaller scholars I used to bring to school and take home on my back, not daring to trust them on the slippery plank.' Once he fell into the mire with a child in his arms and lost 'both overshoes'.
evidence.locator: p. 94, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12682-12701 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In the fall of 1832 John Watkins, from New York, was employed to teach a subscription school on the North Side 'in a log house about twelve feet square'; in his first quarter he had only twelve pupils.
evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12159-12164 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Granville T. Sproat of Boston opened a school in 1833 in the second storey of the Baptist church, a frame building at South Water and Franklin; it 'was a very pleasant one, the pupils obedient and attentive'.
evidence.locator: p. 92-93, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12536-12551 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The school section, the square mile between State and Halsted, Madison and Twelfth, was sold in October 1833 for $38,865. 'The sale was a great mistake': the blocks would have brought 'a hundred times more had they been held twenty years'.
evidence.locator: p. 93, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12561-12580 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The household, its question about a child of five or ten, the route, what is written down or copied, the endings, the timing inputs and the A Schooling Note keepsake are invented connective narrative. No pupil, teacher, fee or answer is documented, and no named person is met.
